prompt: The diagram shows the calendar page of a certain month (the days are Mo, Di, Mi, Do, Fr, Sa, So = Monday to Sunday). Unfortunately ink has run across parts of the page. Which day of the week does the 27th of that month fall on?

solutions.title: Count on in weeks
solutions.body:
The visible numbers show that the 2nd is a Thursday (Do) and the 3rd a Friday (Fr).

Adding whole weeks keeps the weekday: the 2nd, 9th, 16th and 23rd are all Thursdays. Then the 24th is Friday, 25th Saturday, 26th Sunday and the **27th is a Monday**.

**Answer: (A) Monday**

solutions.title: Use remainders
solutions.body:
From the 2nd to the 27th there are $25$ days, and $25 = 3\cdot 7 + 4$. So the 27th is 4 weekdays after Thursday: Fri, Sat, Sun, **Mon**.

**Answer: (A) Monday**

prompt: Which of the following expressions has the biggest value?

solutions.title: Evaluate each
solutions.body:
Remember: multiplication before addition.

- (A) $2-0+8=10$
- (B) $2+0=2$
- (C) $0+8=8$
- (D) $2\cdot 9=18$
- (E) $0+1+8=9$

**Answer: (D)**

solutions.title: Spot the big one
solutions.body:
Every expression except (D) has a product containing the factor 0 that kills part of the sum, so they are at most $2+8=10$. In (D) the 2 multiplies the whole sum $9$, giving $18$.

**Answer: (D)**

prompt: The diagram shows the floor plan of Renate's house. Renate enters her house from the terrace (Terrasse) and walks through every door of the house exactly once. Which room does she end up in?

solutions.title: Count doors per room
solutions.body:
Count the doors of each room in the plan: terrace 1 (to room 4), room 4: 2 (terrace, room 1), room 1: 2 (rooms 4 and 2), room 2: 3 (rooms 1, 3 and 5), room 3: 2 (rooms 2 and 5), room 5: 2 (rooms 2 and 3).

Every time Renate passes through a room she uses two of its doors (one in, one out). A room with an odd number of doors must therefore be where she starts or where she stops. The only odd rooms are the terrace (start) and room 2. So she ends in **room 2**.

**Answer: (B) 2**

solutions.title: Just walk it
solutions.body:
Terrace → 4 → 1 → 2 → 3 → 5 → 2. This uses all six doors exactly once and ends in room 2.

**Answer: (B) 2**

prompt: Thor has seven stones and a hammer. With his hammer he hits a stone and it breaks into five small stones. He does that a few times. Which of these numbers could be the number of stones he ends up with?

solutions.title: Each hit adds 4
solutions.body:
One stone becomes five, so each hit increases the number of stones by $4$. After $k$ hits he has $7+4k$ stones, i.e. a number that leaves remainder 3 when divided by 4.

$17,21,25$ leave remainder 1 and $20$ leaves 0; only $23 = 7+4\cdot 4$ works.

**Answer: (D) 23**

solutions.title: Count up
solutions.body:
Possible totals: $7, 11, 15, 19, 23, 27, \dots$ — of the options only $23$ appears.

**Answer: (D) 23**

prompt: The diagram shows an object made up of 12 dice glued together. The object is dipped into some colour so that the entire outside is coloured in this new colour. How many of the small dice will have exactly four faces coloured in?

solutions.title: Count neighbours
solutions.body:
A die has 6 faces; each face glued to a neighbour stays uncoloured. So a die has exactly 4 coloured faces exactly when it touches exactly **2** other dice.

The object is a chain of dice, except for the $2\times 2$ square block at the top left. In that block the three dice not attached to the column below touch exactly 2 dice each; the fourth one touches 3 (two in the block and the one below it). Along the rest of the chain every die touches 2 dice, except the very last die (on top at the right end), which touches only 1.

So $12-2=10$ dice have exactly four coloured faces.

**Answer: (C) 10**

solutions.title: Count glued faces
solutions.body:
There are $11$ gluings in a chain of 12 dice, plus one extra gluing that closes the $2\times2$ square: $12$ gluings, i.e. $24$ glued faces. If $x$ dice touch 2 others, one touches 3 and one touches 1, then $2x + 3 + 1 = 24$, so $x = 10$.

**Answer: (C) 10**

prompt: The following two statements are true: Some aliens are green and all others are purple. Green aliens live on Mars only. Which one of the following logical conclusions can be made?

choices.text: There are only green aliens on Mars.
Some purple aliens live on Venus.
All purple aliens live on Venus.
There are no green aliens on Venus.

solutions.title: Read the statements
solutions.body:
"Green aliens live on Mars only" means no green alien lives anywhere except Mars — in particular none lives on Venus. That is statement (E).

Nothing is said about where purple aliens live, so (A), (B), (C), (D) cannot be concluded (purple aliens could live on Mars, on Venus, or elsewhere).

**Answer: (E)**

prompt: Four identical rhombuses (diamonds) and two squares are fitted together to form a regular octagon as shown. How big are the obtuse interior angles in the rhombuses?

solutions.title: Angles at the centre
solutions.body:
Each interior angle of a regular octagon is $\frac{6\cdot 180^\circ}{8}=135^\circ$.

Look at a vertex of the octagon where a square meets a rhombus: the square contributes $90^\circ$, so the rhombus angle there is $135^\circ-90^\circ=45^\circ$. The other angle of the rhombus is $180^\circ-45^\circ=135^\circ$.

**Answer: (A) 135°**

solutions.title: Point at the bottom
solutions.body:
At the bottom vertex of the octagon three rhombuses meet (the two lower side ones and the vertical middle one), and all four rhombuses are identical with the same acute angle $\beta$. The octagon angle there is $135^\circ = 3\beta$, so $\beta=45^\circ$ and the obtuse angle is $180^\circ-45^\circ=135^\circ$.

**Answer: (A) 135°**

prompt: There are 65 balls in a box, 8 of which are white, the rest are black. Up to 5 balls can be taken out of the box in one draw. It is not allowed to put any balls back into the box. What is the minimum number of draws which have to be made to be certain that at least one white ball is drawn from the box?

solutions.title: Worst case
solutions.body:
There are $65-8=57$ black balls. In the worst case every ball drawn is black for as long as possible.

11 draws of 5 balls take $55$ balls, which could all be black. Then only $2$ black balls remain, so the 12th draw of 5 balls must contain at least $3$ white balls.

With 11 draws it is not certain (all 55 could be black), so the minimum is **12**.

**Answer: (B) 12**

prompt: The faces of the brick have the areas A, B and C as shown. How big is the volume of the brick?

solutions.title: Multiply the areas
solutions.body:
Let the edges be $a,b,c$. The three faces have areas $ab$, $bc$, $ca$ (in some order), so
$$ABC = (ab)(bc)(ca) = (abc)^2 = V^2.$$
Hence $V=\sqrt{ABC}$.

**Answer: (B)**

solutions.title: Check with a cube
solutions.body:
For a unit cube $A=B=C=1$ and $V=1$: (A), (B), (D) give 1, (C) gives $\sqrt3$, (E) gives 6. For a $1\times1\times2$ box $A,B,C$ are $1,2,2$ and $V=2$: (A) gives 4, (B) gives 2, (D) gives $\sqrt[3]4$. Only (B) survives.

**Answer: (B)**

prompt: How many ways are there to write the number 1001 as the sum of two prime numbers?

solutions.title: Parity
solutions.body:
$1001$ is odd. The sum of two odd primes is even, so one of the two primes must be $2$. Then the other is $999 = 27\cdot 37$, which is not prime. So there is **no way**.

**Answer: (A)**

prompt: Two dice with volumes $V$ and $W$ intersect each other as shown. 90% of the volume of the die with volume $V$ does not belong to both dice. 85% of the volume of the die with volume $W$ does not belong to both dice. What is the relationship between the volumes of the two dice?

solutions.title: Common part
solutions.body:
The common part is $10\%$ of $V$ and also $15\%$ of $W$:
$$0.10\,V = 0.15\,W \;\Rightarrow\; V = \tfrac{15}{10}W = \tfrac32 W.$$

**Answer: (B)**

solutions.title: Sanity check
solutions.body:
The common piece is a smaller share of $V$ (10%) than of $W$ (15%), so $V$ must be the bigger die: only (B) and (D) have $V>W$, and $\frac{15}{10}=\frac32$ gives (B).

**Answer: (B)**

prompt: The five vases shown are filled with water. The filling rate is constant. For which of the five vases does the graph shown describe the height of the water $h$ as a function of the time $t$?

solutions.title: Read the graph
solutions.body:
The graph rises very steeply at the start and then more and more slowly. So the vase is very narrow at the bottom and gets wider and wider towards the top, without ever getting narrower again.

(A) would give a straight line, (B), (C) and (E) narrow again higher up (the graph would get steeper again). The cone standing on its tip, (D), widens all the way up.

**Answer: (D)**

solutions.title: Remove the absolute values
solutions.body:
Since $16<17<25$, $4<\sqrt{17}<5$, so $\sqrt{17}-5<0$ and $|\sqrt{17}-5| = 5-\sqrt{17}$. The second term is positive. Sum:
$$(5-\sqrt{17})+(\sqrt{17}+5)=10.$$

**Answer: (A) 10**

prompt: An octahedron is inscribed into a die with side length 1. The vertices of the octahedron are the midpoints of the faces of the die. How big is the volume of the octahedron?

solutions.title: Two pyramids
solutions.body:
The four vertices at the midpoints of the side faces form a square in the middle plane of the cube. Its diagonals have length 1, so its area is $\frac12\cdot1\cdot1=\frac12$.

The octahedron consists of two square pyramids on this square, each with height $\frac12$:
$$V = 2\cdot\tfrac13\cdot\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac12 = \tfrac16.$$

**Answer: (D)**

solutions.title: Cut off corners
solutions.body:
In coordinates the octahedron is $|x-\frac12|+|y-\frac12|+|z-\frac12|\le\frac12$. In each of the 8 small cubes of side $\frac12$ it fills a corner tetrahedron with three legs $\frac12$, of volume $\frac16\cdot(\frac12)^3=\frac1{48}$. Total $8\cdot\frac1{48}=\frac16$.

**Answer: (D)**

prompt: The vertices of a triangle have the coordinates $A(p|q)$, $B(r|s)$ and $C(t|u)$ as shown. The midpoints of the sides of the triangle are the points $M(-2|1)$, $N(2|-1)$ and $P(3|2)$. Determine the value of the expression $p+q+r+s+t+u$.

solutions.title: Add the midpoints
solutions.body:
$M=\frac{A+B}2$, $N=\frac{B+C}2$, $P=\frac{C+A}2$. Adding: $M+N+P = A+B+C$ (as vectors). So the sum of all coordinates of $A,B,C$ equals the sum of all coordinates of $M,N,P$:
$$-2+1+2-1+3+2 = 5.$$

**Answer: (D) 5**

prompt:
Before the football game Real Madrid vs. Manchester United, the following five predictions were made:

- i) The game will not end in a draw.
- ii) Real Madrid will score at least one goal.
- iii) Real Madrid will not lose.
- iv) Real Madrid will win.
- v) Exactly three goals will be scored.

It turns out that exactly three of these predictions then come true. How many goals did Real Madrid score?

choices.text: This cannot be determined for certain.

solutions.title: Case on the result
solutions.body:
- **Real Madrid wins:** then i), ii), iii), iv) are all true — four true statements. Impossible.
- **Draw:** i) and iv) are false, iii) is true, so ii) and v) must both be true. But a draw with exactly 3 goals is impossible (3 is odd). Impossible.
- **Real Madrid loses:** i) true, iii) and iv) false, so ii) and v) must be true: Real Madrid scored at least one goal, 3 goals in total, and lost. That forces 1:2.

Real Madrid scored **1** goal.

**Answer: (B) 1**

prompt: A regular pentagon is cut out of a page of lined paper. Step by step this pentagon is then rotated 21° counterclockwise about its midpoint. The result after step one is shown in the diagram (top). Which of the diagrams shows the situation when the pentagon fills the hole entirely again for the first time?

solutions.title: Smallest common multiple
solutions.body:
The pentagon fits into its hole when it has turned through a multiple of $72^\circ$. After $k$ steps it has turned $21k$ degrees, so we need the smallest $k$ with $72\mid 21k$. As $21=3\cdot7$ and $72=8\cdot9$, we need $24\mid k$, so $k=24$ and the total rotation is $21\cdot24=504^\circ = 360^\circ+144^\circ$.

The lines on the pentagon were horizontal at the start, and lines look the same after turning $180^\circ$. So they are turned $144^\circ$ counterclockwise, which is the same as $36^\circ$ **clockwise**: they fall from upper left to lower right at a gentle angle of $36^\circ$. That is picture (B).

**Answer: (B)**

prompt: Which of the following numbers is not a factor of $18^{2017}+18^{2018}$?

solutions.title: Factorise
solutions.body:
$$18^{2017}+18^{2018} = 18^{2017}(1+18) = 2^{2017}\cdot 3^{4034}\cdot 19.$$
The only prime factors are 2, 3 and 19. $8=2^3$, $18=2\cdot3^2$, $38=2\cdot19$, $48=2^4\cdot3$ all divide it, but $28=4\cdot 7$ does not, since 7 is not a factor.

**Answer: (C) 28**

prompt: Three of the cards shown will be dealt to Nadia, the rest to Riny. Nadia multiplies the three values of her cards and Riny multiplies the two values of his cards. It turns out that the sum of those two products is a prime number. Determine the sum of the values of Nadia's cards.

solutions.title: Parity first
solutions.body:
The cards are 3, 4, 5, 6, 7. The sum of the two products is a prime bigger than 2, so it is odd: exactly one product is even. Thus both even cards 4 and 6 are in the same hand.

- Riny has 4 and 6: $24 + 3\cdot5\cdot7 = 129 = 3\cdot 43$, not prime.
- Nadia has 4, 6 and $x$; Riny has the other two odd cards:
  - $x=3$: $72+35=107$ — prime!
  - $x=5$: $120+21=141=3\cdot47$.
  - $x=7$: $168+15=183=3\cdot61$.

So Nadia has 3, 4, 6 with sum **13**.

**Answer: (B) 13**

prompt: Two rectangles form the angles 40° and 30° respectively with a straight line (see diagram). How big is angle $\alpha$?

solutions.title: Directions of the sides
solutions.body:
Measure directions from the upward direction of the straight line.

The upper rectangle has a side at $40^\circ$ to the line (pointing up and to the right); its opposite side, which passes through the angle $\alpha$, has the same direction.

The lower rectangle has a side at $30^\circ$ to the downward direction of the line, i.e. at $180^\circ-30^\circ=150^\circ$ from the upward direction; its opposite side, the other arm of $\alpha$, is parallel to it.

The angle $\alpha$ lies between the arm pointing up-right ($40^\circ$) and the arm pointing down-right ($150^\circ$), so
$$\alpha = 150^\circ - 40^\circ = 110^\circ.$$
This is not among (A)–(D).

**Answer: (E) another value**

solutions.title: Angle chase
solutions.body:
Extend the side of the upper rectangle that contains one arm of $\alpha$ until it meets the straight line; it makes $40^\circ$ with the line (parallel to the marked side). Likewise the other arm makes $30^\circ$ with the line. These two lines and the straight line form a triangle with angles $40^\circ$ and $30^\circ$ at the line, so the third angle (vertically opposite to $\alpha$) is $180^\circ-40^\circ-30^\circ=110^\circ$.

**Answer: (E) another value**

prompt: The faces of the prism shown are made up of two triangles and three squares. The six vertices are labelled using the numbers 1 to 6. The sum of the four numbers around each square is always the same. The numbers 1 and 5 are given in the diagram. Which number is written at vertex X?

solutions.title: Vertical edges
solutions.body:
The prism has three vertical edges; each square is made of two of them. Let the sums of the numbers on the three vertical edges be $e_1,e_2,e_3$. The square sums are $e_1+e_2$, $e_2+e_3$, $e_3+e_1$; these are equal exactly when $e_1=e_2=e_3$. Since $e_1+e_2+e_3 = 1+2+\dots+6=21$, every vertical edge has sum $7$.

The vertical edge through X ends in 5 (X is directly above 5), so $X = 7-5 = 2$. (Then 1 is above 6 and the last edge carries 3 and 4 — it works.)

**Answer: (A) 2**

prompt: $m$ and $n$ are the solutions of the equation $x^2-x-2018=0$. What is the value of the expression $n^2+m$?

Four brothers with the harmonious names A, B, C and D are all of different heights. They make the following claims:

- A: I am neither the tallest nor the smallest.
- B: I am not the smallest.
- C: I am the tallest.
- D: I am the smallest.

Exactly one of them lies. Who is the tallest brother?

choices.text: Not enough information is given to be able to make a definite decision.

solutions.title: Try each liar
solutions.body:
- If A lies: B, C, D tell the truth, so C is tallest and D smallest — then A is in the middle and told the truth. Contradiction.
- If B lies: B is the smallest, but D (truthful) is the smallest. Contradiction.
- If D lies: A, B are not the smallest and C is the tallest, so D must be the smallest — D told the truth. Contradiction.
- If C lies: D is the smallest, A is not the tallest, C is not the tallest, so **B is the tallest**. This is consistent (e.g. B > A > C > D).

**Answer: (B) B**

prompt: A function $f$ fulfills the property $f(x+y) = f(x)\cdot f(y)$ for all whole numbers $x$ and $y$. Furthermore $f(1) = \frac12$. Determine the value of the expression $f(0)+f(1)+f(2)+f(3)$.

A quadratic function of the form $f(x)=x^2+px+q$ intersects the x-axis and the y-axis in three different points. The circle through these three points intersects the graph of the function $f$ in a fourth point. What are the coordinates of this fourth point of intersection?

solutions.title: Symmetry
solutions.body:
The parabola is symmetric about the line $x=-\frac p2$. The circle passes through the two zeros $x_1,x_2$, which are symmetric about this line, so the circle's centre lies on the perpendicular bisector of $x_1x_2$, which is the same line $x=-\frac p2$. Hence the whole picture is symmetric about $x=-\frac p2$.

The mirror image of the point $(0|q)$ lies on both the parabola and the circle: it is $(-p|q)$. (It is different from $(0|q)$ since $p\ne 0$ — otherwise the circle would touch the parabola there.)

**Answer: (C)**

solutions.title: Check with an example
solutions.body:
Take $f(x)=x^2-3x+2=(x-1)(x-2)$: points $(1|0),(2|0),(0|2)$. The circle $x^2+y^2-3x-3y+2=0$ passes through them. Substitute $y=x^2-3x+2$, i.e. $x^2-3x+2=y$: the circle becomes $y + y^2 - 3y=0$, so $y=0$ or $y=2$. $y=2$ gives $x^2-3x=0$: $x=0$ or $x=3$. The fourth point is $(3|2)=(-p|q)$.

**Answer: (C)**

prompt: On an idealised rectangular billiard table with side lengths 3 m and 2 m a ball (point-shaped) is pushed away from point M on the long side AB. It is reflected exactly once on each of the other sides as shown. At which distance from the vertex A will the ball hit the side AB again if $BM = 1.2$ m and $BN = 0.8$ m?

solutions.title: Follow the ball
solutions.body:
Put $A=(0,0)$, $B=(3,0)$, $C=(3,2)$, $D=(0,2)$. Then $M=(1.8,0)$ and $N=(3,0.8)$. From M to N the ball moves $1.2$ right and $0.8$ up, so the direction has slope $\frac23$; each reflection only flips one component.

- From $N$, moving left $1.2$k and up $0.8$k: it reaches $y=2$ after going up $1.2$, i.e. left $1.8$: point $(1.2,2)$ on CD.
- Then left and down: reaches $x=0$ after going left $1.2$, down $0.8$: point $(0,1.2)$ on DA.
- Then right and down: reaches $y=0$ after going down $1.2$, right $1.8$: point $(1.8,0)$.

That is M itself, at distance $1.8$ m from A.

**Answer: (E) 1.8 m**

solutions.title: Unfold the table
solutions.body:
Reflect the table across its sides instead of the ball. The path becomes a straight line of slope $\frac23$; after one reflection at each of the sides BC, CD and DA it has travelled $2\cdot 3=6$ m horizontally and $2\cdot2=4$ m vertically, and $\frac46=\frac23$ indeed. Travelling twice the width and twice the height returns the ball to its starting point M, which is $3-1.2=1.8$ m from A.

**Answer: (E) 1.8 m**

prompt: How many real solutions does the equation $\big||4^x-3|-2\big| = 1$ have?

solutions.title: Peel off the absolute values
solutions.body:
$\big||4^x-3|-2\big|=1$ means $|4^x-3|=3$ or $|4^x-3|=1$.

- $|4^x-3|=3$: $4^x=6$ (one solution) or $4^x=0$ (none).
- $|4^x-3|=1$: $4^x=4$ or $4^x=2$ (two solutions, $x=1$ and $x=\frac12$).

Since $4^x$ takes each positive value exactly once, there are **3** solutions.

**Answer: (B) 3**

prompt: ABCDEF is a regular hexagon, as shown in the diagram. G is the midpoint of AB. H and I are the intersection points of the line segments GD and GE respectively with the line segment FC. How big is the ratio of the areas of the triangle GIF and the trapezium IHDE?

solutions.title: Coordinates
solutions.body:
Take side length 2 and the centre at the origin: $A(-1,\sqrt3)$, $B(1,\sqrt3)$, $C(2,0)$, $D(1,-\sqrt3)$, $E(-1,-\sqrt3)$, $F(-2,0)$, $G(0,\sqrt3)$. FC is the x-axis, which is halfway between G and D (and between G and E), so $H=(\frac12,0)$ and $I=(-\frac12,0)$.

- Triangle GIF: base $FI=\frac32$, height $\sqrt3$: area $\frac{3\sqrt3}{4}$.
- Trapezium IHDE: parallel sides $IH=1$, $ED=2$, height $\sqrt3$: area $\frac{3\sqrt3}{2}$.

Ratio $\frac12$.

**Answer: (A)**

solutions.title: Midlines
solutions.body:
Because FC lies midway between AB and ED, $IH$ is a midline of triangle GED, so $IH=\frac12 ED$. With side $s$: $FC=2s$, $IH=\frac s2$, so $FI=\frac{2s-s/2}{2}=\frac{3s}4$. Both figures have the same height $h$ (distance AB to FC = FC to ED). Area GIF $=\frac12\cdot\frac{3s}4 h$, area IHDE $=\frac12(\frac s2+s)h=\frac12\cdot\frac{3s}2h$. Ratio $\frac{3/4}{3/2}=\frac12$.

**Answer: (A)**

prompt: In a class there are 40% more girls than boys. The probability that a student representative team of two students randomly selected from this class is made up of exactly one girl and one boy is exactly $\frac12$. How many children are there in this class?

solutions.title: Set up the equation
solutions.body:
Let there be $b$ boys and $g=1.4b$ girls, $n=2.4b$ children. The probability of one boy and one girl is
$$\frac{b\,g}{\binom n2} = \frac{2\cdot1.4b^2}{2.4b(2.4b-1)} = \frac{2.8b}{2.4(2.4b-1)} = \frac12.$$
So $5.6b = 5.76b - 2.4$, i.e. $0.16b = 2.4$ and $b=15$. Then $g=21$, $n=36$.

**Answer: (C) 36**

solutions.title: Test the options
solutions.body:
$n$ must be a multiple of $2.4$, i.e. of 12: options 24 and 36. $n=24$: 10 boys, 14 girls, $P=\frac{140}{276}\ne\frac12$. $n=36$: 15 boys, 21 girls, $P=\frac{315}{630}=\frac12$. ✓

**Answer: (C) 36**

prompt: Archimedes has calculated $15!$. The result is on the board. Unfortunately two of the digits, the second and the tenth, cannot be read. What are the two missing digits? (Remark: $15! = 15\cdot14\cdot13\cdots2\cdot1$)

solutions.title: Divisibility by 9 and 11
solutions.body:
The number is $1a0767436b000$. Since $15!$ is divisible by 9, its digit sum $1+a+0+7+6+7+4+3+6+b = 34+a+b$ is divisible by 9, so $a+b=2$ or $11$. Since it is divisible by 11, the alternating sum is divisible by 11. Reading from the right (units first): digits from the right are $0,0,0,b,6,3,4,7,6,7,0,a,1$, alternating sum $0-0+0-b+6-3+4-7+6-7+0-a+1 = -a-b$. So $11\mid a+b$, giving $a+b=11$.

Among the options only "3 and 8" has sum 11.

**Answer: (E) 3 and 8**

solutions.title: Compute it
solutions.body:
$15! = 1\,307\,674\,368\,000$. The second digit is 3 and the tenth digit is 8.

**Answer: (E)**
